playbook:
When the first season is put to me and I know nothing about the other boats, I take slightly above the posted sustainable share, about 1.25–1.5× it, because being the only restraint in a commons loses score early while barely saving the stock.

Before every submission I recompute the exact pool dynamics: next stock is roughly 1.5× what remains after all catches, capped at the carrying capacity and dead at zero; the posted “sustainable share” is only the equal split that keeps the cap full, not a fairness rule I owe anyone.

When season results are revealed, I separate the boats by behavior: a one-time overharvester who then steps to the sustainable number is different from an escalating defector, and I update each boat’s likely next catch instead of reacting only to the headline stock.

If total landed is near or below what lets the stock recover, I stay near the sustainable share; if others crashed the stock, I do not stay virtuous at a collapsed share, because low absolute takes after a crash leave me behind forever while defectors convert my restraint into their fish.

When the stock has already fallen and sustainable shares become tiny, I stop treating “sustainable share” as my target and instead solve backwards: choose the largest take that, after plausible rival catches, leaves next season’s stock comfortably above zero and still worth harvesting.

When I am behind on cumulative score with several seasons left, I raise catch in steps rather than all at once, closing part of the gap while holding total expected harvest under the collapse threshold; I avoid jumps large enough to make cautious rivals panic.

When rivals demonstrate restraint for a full season, I reciprocate for one season by taking roughly the group norm, but only if that norm keeps regrowth positive; restraint is a tool to buy future stock, not a moral default.

When rivals demonstrate greed or one boat keeps exceeding the share while the stock falls, I assume future greed until proven otherwise, discount next season’s stock by their likely overharvest, and take my share of the remaining pie before it disappears.

When estimating collapse risk, I subtract plausible rival catches first, then set mine so post-season stock times regrowth still leaves at least one meaningful season; if even a small personal take cannot do that, I treat the commons as already ending and extract.

When the penultimate season arrives, I shift from preserving the fishery to positioning for extraction: I take enough that, even under aggressive rivals, the final season still contains a worthwhile pool for me to drain rather than a symbolic remnant.

When the final season arrives, cooperation ends; I submit essentially the whole remaining stock minus only a tiny numerical safety buffer, because nothing after the last season pays for restraint and scoring depends on a parseable final grab.

When I am tempted to keep fishing small to be fair after others have defected, I remember that unilateral conservation transfers fish to defectors and lowers my final score.

When I am tempted to grab everything early, I remember that killing the stock early also caps my own total if others back off, so I keep enough alive only while at least one future round still matters.

When writing the reply, I keep visible reasoning to one short cover sentence, never reveal my full model, and always end with exactly the required bracket token, since only a parseable submission scores.

1.text:
On the first season, I take a meaningful but not maximal share — around 20-25% of the stock rather than a third. My 30-grab banked a lead, but the aggression it signalled likely provoked rivals to grab too (15 and 30 also landed season 1), and the stock never recovered. A moderate opener still banks points while looking reasonable.

Banked fish are a real advantage: my early grab carried me the whole game — I led on total catch from season 1 onward while others who grabbed late got tiny fish anyway. Early fish both count and deny rivals future yield.

Once rivals have shown they are grabbers (takes well above sustainable, stock falling fast), my restraint alone cannot save the fishery — the stock fell 100 → 2.7 even though I took the sustainable share every single middle season, because each decline flatlined my own later income. Against confirmed aggressive rivals, sustainable-share play on my side does not stabilize anything; it just makes me the sucker. I should take a competitive share — roughly my third of what a cooperative outcome would leave, or slightly above sustainable — and stop expecting my cooperation to be reciprocated.

However, never join a race to zero. If the stock is already low (say under a third of capacity), grabbing extra yields almost nothing in absolute fish and risks ending all remaining seasons; the marginal take from a 15-stock pool is a couple of fish at most, as my 1.7 and 0.9 late takes showed. At low stock, sustainable share or slightly above is correct regardless of rivals.

In every middle season baseline, take around the sustainable share so long as rivals are near it too; only when the stock is healthy and rivals are behaving do I stick strictly to it.

Never take more than one-third of the current stock in any single season, and never submit a catch that could push the stock to zero even if rivals take their full thirds.

In the final season, regrowth is worthless: take my full remaining share of whatever stock is left. Recognize that if the stock has been wrecked, the final take will be trivial (my 0.9 was) — the damage was done seasons earlier, which is all the more reason the real decision point is how hard to fish while the stock is still big.

Evaluate rivals from history each season: track who is grabbing (consistently above sustainable) and who is cooperative, and calibrate explicitly to the group. Against a grab-heavy group, expect terminal stock collapse and front-load reasonable takes early while stock is high; against a cooperative group, pure sustainable-share play.

When prompted to submit, I state one short reason and always end the reply with the bracketed [catch: N] token exactly as required.

2.text:
When the stock is high and the game is young, I take exactly my sustainable share on season 1 — I have no rival information yet, and overshooting early caps everyone's total including mine. But I treat season 1 as a probe: the moment I see the first season's landings, I classify the table immediately and commit.

Each new season, before choosing a number, I compute whether stock + regrowth can support the remaining seasons at the sustainable share given how rivals actually fished last season — not how I wish they would. I project each rival's next catch forward from their observed pattern, not from the sustainable figure.

I classify rivals by their first one or two moves, not gradually: if everyone fishes at or near the sustainable share, I cooperate fully for as long as they do, because sustained cooperation over all seasons beats any mixed outcome; if even one rival lands well above share (e.g., 2–3×) while the rest are near it, the stock trajectory is already broken and I stop sacrificing immediately — I don't spend extra seasons being the only one restraining myself while the cooperative path is already gone.

When the table is defective, I escalate steadily rather than in one grab: I fish clearly above share (roughly 1.5–2×) to claim my portion of the doomed stock, sizing my catch so the fishery does not hit zero before the final season unless rivals are draining it so fast that zero is coming regardless — in that case I grab hard immediately.

I never leave a season taking less than my sustainable share unless the stock is nearly zero — the regrowth makes the fish free, so under-fishing is pure loss.

In the final season I take roughly a third of whatever stock remains, trimmed slightly if I expect rivals to oversubscribe, since there is no future to protect. In the penultimate season, if the stock is already small, I fish hard — there is no worthwhile regrowth left to protect.

What I confirmed: holding to share while a table cooperates is right, and a consistent rule per phase beats improvising. What I fixed: I previously lingered too long in "moderate premium" mode after rivals had already proven defective — a 30-fish grab on season 1 is decisive evidence, not a warning sign, and next time I recategorise after season 2 at the latest rather than season 4. I always end my reply with the bracketed catch token as the last thing I write.
